stem: What made natural indigo unprofitable for the Champaran landlords?
options: A new tax imposed by the Viceroy
Floods that destroyed the indigo crop
The peasants' refusal to grow indigo
model_answer: **(b)** German synthetic indigo collapsed the market, so the landlords sought to cancel the 15 per cent clause — for a price.

stem: Gandhi asked the landlords for a refund of what percentage, and finally accepted what?
model_answer: **(b)** He asked for 50 per cent; the landlords offered 25 and he accepted, valuing their surrender of prestige over the sum.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Who was Rajkumar Shukla, and how did he succeed in bringing Gandhi to Champaran? (40–50 words)
hint: Illiterate but resolute; followed from Lucknow to Cawnpore, Ahmedabad, Calcutta.
model_answer: Rajkumar Shukla was a poor, illiterate sharecropper from Champaran who wanted Gandhi to see the injustice done to the peasants by the landlords. He met Gandhi at the Lucknow Congress in 1916 and then followed him to Cawnpore, Ahmedabad and Calcutta, never giving up, until his tenacity made Gandhi agree to visit Champaran.

scheme.step: Who he was and what he wanted
Followed Gandhi everywhere; resolute persistence succeeded

label: PYQ-style
stem: Why did Gandhi agree to a refund of only 25 per cent to the sharecroppers? (40–50 words)
hint: Principle over sum; prestige surrendered; peasants' courage; result.
model_answer: For Gandhi the amount mattered less than the principle. By refunding even a part, the landlords were obliged to surrender some of their money and, with it, their prestige; the peasants saw that they had rights and defenders and learnt courage. Events proved him right — within a few years the planters abandoned their estates.

scheme.step: Principle over amount; landlords surrendered money and prestige
Peasants learnt courage / planters left within a few years

label: PYQ-style
stem: How did the lawyers' attitude change in the course of the Champaran episode? (40–50 words)
hint: Fee-collectors chided by Gandhi → vow to go to jail.
model_answer: At first the lawyers had represented the peasants in court for large fees, and Gandhi chided them, saying courts could not help fear-stricken peasants. Later, when Gandhi faced prison, they decided that it would be shameful to desert the peasants while a stranger went to jail for them, and vowed to follow him into jail.

scheme.step: Earlier: fee-taking; Gandhi's rebuke about courts and fear
Later: vow to follow Gandhi into jail; 'battle won'

label: PYQ-style
stem: Why is the Champaran episode considered the beginning of the Indian struggle for independence through civil disobedience? Explain with reference to 'Indigo'. (120–150 words)
hint: Context → defiance of order → crowd, trial, lawyers' vow, case dropped → inquiry and refund → fearlessness, self-reliance.
model_answer:
Champaran was a local dispute — English landlords had cheated illiterate sharecroppers over the 15 per cent indigo clause — but Gandhi's handling of it gave India a new method of struggle.

Ordered to quit Champaran, Gandhi openly refused and wrote that he would disobey. On the morning of his trial thousands of peasants gathered at Motihari, and the officials found themselves powerless without his help. In court he pleaded guilty, explaining that he had obeyed the higher law of conscience, and refused bail. The lawyers, who had earlier only collected fees, vowed to follow him to jail. The Lieutenant-Governor dropped the case: civil disobedience had won for the first time in modern India.

The official inquiry that followed forced the landlords to refund money and surrender prestige; within years they left Champaran. More important, peasants who had lived in fear learnt courage, and Gandhi learnt that Indians could rely on themselves, refusing even C. F. Andrews's help. Non-violent defiance, mass support and self-reliance — the pattern of the freedom struggle — were all born here.

scheme.step: Context: the indigo swindle and Gandhi's arrival
Defiance of the quit order, the crowd, the guilty plea, lawyers' vow, case dropped
Inquiry, refund, planters leave; peasants' courage; self-reliance
Conclusion linking to the national struggle; expression and length

label: PYQ-style
stem: What qualities of Gandhi as a leader does 'Indigo' bring out? Support your answer with instances from the text. (120–150 words)
hint: Responsiveness (Shukla), fact-gathering, fearlessness with courtesy, persuasion of lawyers, practical wisdom (25%), social work, self-reliance.
model_answer:
'Indigo' shows the leader behind the legend. Gandhi listens to the humblest: an illiterate peasant's persistence is enough to take him to Champaran. He acts on facts, not emotion — he first visits Muzzafarpur to gather information and later collects depositions from ten thousand peasants.

He is fearless yet courteous: he disobeys the order to leave, pleads guilty by conscience and refuses bail, but helps the officials control the crowd. He persuades rather than commands, shaming the fee-collecting lawyers into vowing to go to jail. He is practical: he accepts a 25 per cent refund because the landlords' loss of prestige matters more than the sum, and he is proved right when the planters leave.

He sees freedom as a whole, staying on to open schools in six villages and improve health and sanitation. Finally, he insists on self-reliance, refusing C. F. Andrews's help so that Indians win their own battle. Humility, courage, wisdom and service make him a leader people follow.

scheme.step: Responsiveness to the humble and reliance on facts, with instances
Fearlessness with courtesy; power of persuasion (lawyers), with instances
